sweep_summary: One title-hit for Western Apache: Hoijer 1943 'Pitch Accent in the Apachean Languages' (Language 19:38-41). The DOI now resolves to Cambridge Core and is paywalled (JSTOR/CUP; OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Unpaywall all report closed), but the whole 1943 volume of Language is openly scanned at archive.org (item sim_language_1943_19, Kraus 1964 reprint); I downloaded the scanned text and the four page scan (pp.38-41) to and checked the p.38 image against the scanned. The article explicitly covers San Carlos (= Western Apache) and states that Apachean utterances are 'a succession of evenly stressed syllables each of which possesses a clearly defined pitch accent or tone', with four syllable tonemes (high, low, falling, rising) and no word- or phrase-level accentual pattern (pp.38-39). This confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding and refines it: it is a first-hand claim of NO word stress, at the Apachean-group level with Navaho examples, which sits beside (and is older than) the catalog's Western-Apache-specific but contested stress notes (Greenfeld 1972/1978 stem stress vs Landar 1980). It does not supersede the language-specific deciding source (WMACC 1972 dictionary front matter) but should be added as the classic supporting citation.

new_statements.quote: An utterance in the Apachean languages, phonetically considered, is a succession of evenly stressed syllables each of which possesses a clearly defined pitch accent or tone. ... there are no distinctive accentual patterns characteristic of the word, the phrase, or the sentence which stand over and above the accentual patterns formed by the succession of syllables constituting the utterance. The only tonemes with which we have to deal, then, are those which belong to the syllable. Four such syllable tonemes are phonemically isolable: (1) the high tone ... (2) the low tone ... (3) the falling tone ... and (4) the rising tone
new_statements.citation: Hoijer, Harry. 1943. Pitch Accent in the Apachean Languages. Language 19(1): 38-41 (DOI 10.2307/410317; read from the Kraus 1964 reprint of vol. 19 scanned at archive.org, item sim_language_1943_19).

new_statements.reading: Hoijer's classic statement for the whole Apachean group (San Carlos/Western Apache named on p.38): the languages are tone languages with a toneme on every syllable (H, L, falling, rising; contour tones only on long vowels/vowel clusters of morphologically complex syllables), and there is no word stress at all — syllables are 'evenly stressed'. This supports the catalog's 'tonal' kind and adds a first-hand negative on word stress that is stronger than the catalog's current secondary note (Greenfeld's predictable stem stress, contested by Landar 1980). Caveats: pooled across six languages, Navaho examples only, 1943.

tone_statements.quote: The spelling of WA is the standard system used and described in White Mountain Apache Culture Center (1972:vii-xii, 107-110) and in Bray (1998:xii-xviii). This standard system only distinguishes high tone (acute accent) and low tone (no accent); the mid tone is usually marked as a low tone, but occasionally it is marked as high tone (acute accent), particularly on a short i or a long ii, or on a long oo (then often written íí). Because of the unsatisfactory marking of the mid tone in the standard system, the following addition to the system is used in this paper: Low tones are unmarked v, vv, mid tones are marked [v with macron], and high tones are marked [v with acute].
